title: Aphids in the Greenhouse
story: A greenhouse keeps seedlings on a grid. Each spot is empty (0), a healthy plant (1) or a plant with aphids (2). Aphids crawl: each day, every healthy plant directly above, below, left or right of an infested plant becomes infested. Empty spots stop them.
If nobody acts, how many days until every plant is infested? Or are some plants cut off and safe forever?
task: Write daysUntilAllInfested(trays). Return the number of days until no healthy plant is left. Return 0 if there are no healthy plants at the start, and -1 if some healthy plant can never be reached.
All infested plants spread at the same time. A plant infested on day d starts spreading on day d + 1.

examples.explanation: On day 1 the aphids reach (0,1) and (1,0). On day 2 they reach (0,2) and (1,1), on day 3 they reach (2,1), and on day 4 they reach (2,2). Every plant is infested after 4 days.

The two infested plants spread at the same time. The left one reaches (0,1) and (1,0) on day 1 and (1,1) on day 2; the right one reaches (0,3) on day 1. The answer is 2, not the 3 or more you get by handling one source after the other.
The empty spot cuts off the plant on the right, so it is never infested and the answer is -1.

hints: In the second example, label every plant with the day it gets infested. Which plants get day 1? Does it matter which infested plant they caught it from?
A plant's day is its step distance to the nearest infested plant. You want shortest distances from a whole set of starting points at once.
Breadth-first search from one start finds distances in rings. What if you put every infested plant in the queue at distance 0 from the start?

Queue every 2 at day 0 and count the healthy plants. Run breadth-first search: each time you infect a healthy neighbor, record its day as the current day + 1, decrement the healthy count and queue it. Return -1 if the count is not 0 at the end, otherwise the largest day recorded (0 if none).
bruteForce: Simulate day by day: copy the grid, infect every healthy plant next to an infested one, and repeat until nothing changes. Then check for healthy plants left.
Each day rescans the grid, and a long winding row of plants can take about one day per plant: up to about 200 days × 400 spots on a 20 × 20 grid. Breadth-first search reaches each plant once.

walkthrough: Each plant is infested on the day equal to its step distance from the nearest infested plant. That is breadth-first search with many starting points: put them all in the first ring and the rings grow from every source at once, like the aphids.
Trace the second example, [[2,1,0,1],[1,1,0,2]]. There are 4 healthy plants, and the day 0 ring is (0,0) and (1,3).
• On day 1, (0,0) infects (0,1) and (1,0), and (1,3) infects (0,3). One healthy plant is left.
• On day 2, the day-1 ring infects (1,1). No healthy plants are left, so the loop stops.
Answer: 2. The loop stops as soon as no healthy plant is left. That avoids the most common bug here: looping until the queue is empty counts one extra day for the last ring, which infects nothing.
The healthy counter covers both edge cases: none at the start gives 0 without entering the loop, and any left unreached give -1.
solution.timeWhy: Each spot is infected at most once, and each one checks four neighbors.
solution.spaceWhy: The solution stores a copy of the grid and the queue holding the current ring.
solution.takeaway: When something spreads from several places at once, start breadth-first search with all the sources in the first ring. One search gives every cell its distance to the nearest source.
